one_liner: Header-only C++20 I/O library replacing iostream/cstdio and std::to_chars with buffered, syscall-near I/O.
what_it_does: fast_io replaces <iostream>/<cstdio> for file, console, and device I/O, and includes its own integer/floating-point formatting (a to_chars/from_chars-like layer). It exposes print()/scan() free functions and buffered file types (obuf_file, ibuf_file, iobuf_file, c_file, native_file_loader) built on a native-handle interface (POSIX fd, Win32 HANDLE, C FILE*), with C++20 concepts used to abstract devices at compile time instead of virtual dispatch. It is not a drop-in replacement for iostream's API, but it interoperates with FILE* and std::stream objects for incremental adoption.
how_it_is_fast: Devices are abstracted through C++20 concepts (static polymorphism), avoiding the vtable dispatch, locale machinery, and sentry-object overhead that <iostream>/streambuf carry on every call. I/O goes through the library's own buffered file objects close to the raw syscall/native-handle level rather than through libc FILE* layering. Integer formatting uses the jeaiii digit-pair method (include/fast_io_core_impl/integers/jeaiii_method.h, the same technique as the jeaiii/itoa sibling entry). Double round-trip formatting is implemented in include/fast_io_unit/floating/roundtrip.h, whose header comment attributes the algorithm to 'Dragonbox' (Jk Jeon) even though the readme's benchmark section calls it the 'Ryu algorithm' — these are different, related fast float-to-string algorithms.
when_to_use: Bulk sequential file I/O (writing/reading millions of integers or lines) where std::fstream or stdio throughput is the bottleneck.
Already on C++20 with a concepts-capable compiler (GCC>=14, Clang>=17, or MSVC per current support.md) and able to adopt a non-drop-in API.
Low-level, embedded, kernel-driver, or freestanding/WASM targets that need direct handle/syscall-level I/O and small binaries (readme's static-link comparison: 155KB fast_io vs 925KB fstream).
Need Unicode-aware (UTF-8/16/32) transcoding I/O in the same layer as raw throughput.
Can accept the Anti-Tivo License's non-standard terms in exchange for the speed.
when_not_to_use: Need a true drop-in replacement for std::iostream or std::to_chars without touching call sites — fast_io's API shape and exceptions-only error model differ substantially.
Legal review requires an OSI-approved permissive or conventional copyleft license — Anti-Tivo License v1.0 is custom and not OSI-approved.
Toolchain can't reach the current minimum (GCC>=14/Clang>=17 per support.md), which is notably newer than the GCC 11/MSVC 19.26 used in the readme's own benchmark numbers.

Need independently reproduced numbers before adopting — all published results are the author's own, with no CPU model or optimization flags stated, and the readme's cited benchmark paths no longer exist in the reorganized benchmark/ directory.

Multithreaded writers by default — the fast unbuffered types are not thread-safe; the thread-safe *_mutex variants give up much of the speed edge (readme: 0.049s to 0.146s output time on MinGW for the mutex variant).

integration.dependencies: none for core I/O (single fast_io.h entry header); optional interop code exists for Boost, Qt, MFC, OpenSSL, LLVM raw_fd_ostream, Lua/Python bindings
integration.min_toolchain: C++20 with concepts; per support.md: GCC>=14, Clang>=17, or MSVC (readme's own benchmarks were run on the older GCC 11.0.0 and MSVC 19.26.28805)
integration.platforms: x86/x86_64, arm/aarch64, riscv/riscv64, powerpc64, mips variants, wasm32-wasi, avr, ia64, loongarch64, xtensa-esp32, and more per support.md; Windows/Linux/BSD/Darwin/iOS/Android, Cygwin/MSYS2/Wine/ReactOS, plus freestanding, kernel-driver, and bootloader targets
integration.thread_safety: Default buffered types (e.g. obuf_file) are not thread-safe; explicit *_mutex variants (obuf_file_mutex, c_file) add thread safety at a measured throughput cost in the readme's own benchmarks
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — explain: constructs from and interoperates with FILE*/iostream objects for gradual adoption, but the print/scan API and exceptions-only error model are a different interface from <iostream>/std::to_chars, not a drop-in replacement

gotchas: readme's cited benchmark source paths (benchmarks/0000.10m_size_t/unit, benchmarks/0001.10m_double/charconv) do not exist in the current repo; benchmark/ has been reorganized into numbered dirs (e.g. 0002.file_io_tsc, 0004.file_io_floating).

readme calls the double round-trip formatting the 'Ryu algorithm', but the implementation header (include/fast_io_unit/floating/roundtrip.h) is commented 'Algorithm: Dragonbox, Author: Jk Jeon' — a different, related algorithm.
MinGW benchmark numbers required the author to patch libstdc++'s BUFSIZ from 512 bytes to 1MB before comparing against fstream; the out-of-the-box gap on stock MinGW would be smaller.
License is the custom Anti-Tivo License v1.0 (non-OSI-approved, GitHub reports it as NOASSERTION) — review it before shipping, it is not a standard permissive or copyleft license.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick fast_io over Boost.Charconv, c4core, fast_double_parser, rigtorp/CharConv, or jeaiii/itoa when the goal is whole-file/stream I/O throughput via buffered file objects and syscall-near handles, not just isolated number<->string conversion — those siblings only replace to_chars/from_chars/stoi/strtod, while fast_io replaces the entire iostream/cstdio layer (and internally reuses jeaiii's itoa method for its own integer formatting).
verified_claims_summary: Author-run benchmarks (no CPU model or optimization flags stated) show fast_io's buffered file I/O beating std::fstream by roughly 6-15x for writing/reading 10 million integers on GCC 11 (Linux and MinGW-W64) and MSVC 19.26, and beating MSVC's std::to_chars(charconv) by about 23% (~1.29x throughput) for round-trip formatting of 10 million doubles, also on MSVC 19.26.
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2026-07-02 on the 'next' branch, 2026-03-13 on master); usability is capped at 'reference' because of the non-OSI Anti-Tivo License, not because of code immaturity — 851 stars and an extensive examples/benchmark/fuzzing tree.
